problem_data.story:
The Supply Chain Sentinel Strikes Back!

Like all corporate crusaders worthy of the title, the Supply Chain Sentinel has an Achilles' heel. In the case of the Supply Chain Sentinel, his Achilles' heel is not related to inventory, logistics, or distribution networks but something less tangible.

An explanation: Last week, the business journal you are currently reading forced the Supply Chain Sentinel at metaphorical gunpoint to read a series of syrupy management books about work-life balance, and then to write about them. The Supply Chain Sentinel, who can withstand hostile takeovers, supply shortages, transportation strikes, and interminable board meetings, almost succumbed to terminal banality after reading these books. Except for one thing: One of the books, The Art of Corporate Mindfulness, which collects and simplifies various philosophies about ethical decision-making in business, got the Supply Chain Sentinel to thinking. This, in a way, is the Supply Chain Sentinel's Achilles' heel: thinking. Perhaps it is wrong, the Supply Chain Sentinel thought, to complain about the petty frustrations and inefficiencies of life in the cutthroat world of economic development. The Supply Chain Sentinel felt that perhaps he should counsel those who write seeking help to meditate, to accept poor vendor service the way one accepts quarterly earnings fluctuations, and to extend a compassionate hand of forgiveness to those who provide inadequate supply chain management.

But then the Supply Chain Sentinel checked his email, and the feeling passed.

The Supply Chain Sentinel does not make light of work-life balance or of the notion that there is more to business than the relentless pursuit of profit margins. If the Supply Chain Sentinel were not, for a corporate crusader, extremely nonjudgmental--as opposed to his alter ego, Samuel Kennedy, who is considered insufferably critical by his colleagues at the Redwood Territory Economic Development Council--the Supply Chain Sentinel would tell the occasional correspondent to let go of their petty grievance and focus on strategic priorities.

But the Supply Chain Sentinel also believes that even the most enlightened business philosopher has never tried to lease warehouse robotics equipment from RoboLease Inc. If they had tried to lease from RoboLease, they never would have achieved operational efficiency. (For the complete back story, see "Supply Chain Sentinel" column episodes one and two.)

The complaints about RoboLease's non-commitment commitment policy continue to pour in through electronic channels. Two correspondents this month shared particularly instructive tales of RoboLease frustration.

The first, Xavier Frank, wrote in with this cautionary tale: "Last month, I went to our facility in Magnolia, Galdoria to help my company install automated sorting systems for our new distribution center. My operations manager had reserved three industrial robotics units from RoboLease for the installation date. I warned him about RoboLease's 'not really a reservation per se' policy that I learned from the Supply Chain Sentinel. He didn't believe such a thing would happen to our company, so he didn't act on my warning. A colleague suggested we have TechLease as a backup option, which seemed like solid advice at the time."

The second correspondent, Nathan Vance, had a remarkably similar experience. Nathan wrote: "After reading your column, I thought I was prepared. When RoboLease failed me—they claimed my 'reserved' units were still being 'calibrated'—I drove straight to TechLease. They had exactly what I needed, and I was operational within hours. Sometimes the backup plan becomes the main plan."

Xavier continues his story--as if you don't know what happened already--"I went to RoboLease with my operations manager to collect our 'reserved' robotics units. The facility had many customers standing around looking frustrated. When we got to the front of the line, the representative informed us that our 'reserved' units had not yet been returned from a previous client. We asked if we could lease some of the many robots sitting idle in their testing bay. The representative laughed and said those units were awaiting software updates that were indefinitely delayed."

At this point, Xavier notes, he and his operations manager faced a choice. "My colleague's TechLease suggestion was still echoing in my mind. But when I called TechLease, they said their nearest available units were in a different region—a twelve-hour drive. We needed equipment that day, not next week."

Xavier and his chastened operations manager then tried a different approach. "We started calling every provider in the area. The account manager at our eventual solution told us they pride themselves on being everything RoboLease is not. They had units available immediately, and we were installing by that afternoon."

The Supply Chain Sentinel is resisting the urge to gloat about Xavier's operations manager learning his lesson about RoboLease.

Meanwhile, Nathan Vance reports complete satisfaction with how his situation resolved at TechLease: "Best decision I ever made was having that backup ready. TechLease treated me like a priority customer from minute one."

The Supply Chain Sentinel has still not received a call from RoboLease spokeswoman Grace Ross explaining why RoboLease refuses to provide robotics equipment to companies who reserve equipment, but the Supply Chain Sentinel is pleased to note that several correspondents have written in over the past month saying that, based on what they have read in this column, they will be taking their business elsewhere.

Xavier, in a follow-up email, wanted to clarify one point for readers: "For anyone in a similar bind, don't assume any single backup will work. TechLease couldn't help me due to geography, but there are other options out there. I found mine at a company I'd never heard of before that day—they call themselves AutomationPro, and they saved my entire installation timeline."

The Supply Chain Sentinel will undoubtedly return to the sorry state of affairs at RoboLease in the next episode, but now on to this month's logistics debacle.

Before we begin, though, the Supply Chain Sentinel nearly forgot to announce the winner of last month's contest, in which readers were asked to answer the question, "What's the difference between supply chain disruptions and incompetent vendors?"

The winner is one Roman Frank, who wrote, "You can plan for supply chain disruptions." Roman is the winner of a year's supply of industrial-grade lubricant for warehouse equipment, and he will receive his prize just as soon as the Supply Chain Sentinel figures out how much lubricant actually constitutes a year's supply. The new contest question: How much industrial lubricant comprises a year's supply of industrial lubricant?

This month's logistics company in the spotlight is SwiftFreight. Loyal readers will recall that last month the Supply Chain Sentinel praised SwiftFreight for its "exemplary" delivery reliability. This brought forth a small number of articulate dissensions. The most articulate, and the most troubling, came from Francesco Reid, who wrote, "Last quarter, shipping a critical order from our Pinehurst, Jarvonia facility to our client in Crestwood, Orvandor with our entire product line (two container loads included), the shipment arrived during a severe weather event. And we waited for confirmation. And waited for confirmation. And waited for confirmation."

Three days later, Francesco says, the confirmation came, "damaged goods reported. We took the documentation to SwiftFreight's claims department and were faced with the most complicated, unclear, and confusing mechanism for filing a claim we experienced shippers have ever seen."

When they finally inspected the shipment, Francesco and his team made a terrible discovery, "We discovered that our products were damaged throughout--the top layer was so compromised that moisture had penetrated down to the lower levels, destroying an entire shipment worth over $200,000. Obviously, our containers had just been sitting exposed on the dock during the storm. To this day, I've never heard a thing from SwiftFreight, despite calls and emails and registered letters."

This, of course, is where the Supply Chain Sentinel steps in. The Supply Chain Sentinel knows that SwiftFreight is different from the average logistics company, in that it doesn't go out of its way to antagonize its paying clients (see: the consciousness studies of customer relations that SwiftFreight supposedly embraces), so I expected a quick and generous resolution to Francesco's problem.

What I got at first, though, was a load of corporate obfuscation.

"The company's policy, which is consistent with all contracts of carriage at all logistics firms, requires that clients file a report in person for lost or damaged shipments within 24 hours of delivery at their destination," a SwiftFreight spokesman, Roberto Hopkins, e-mailed me. "[Francesco Reid] indicates he called for a few days, but did not file a report in person until three days later. SwiftFreight, as a courtesy, took his report anyway and asked for follow-up information and written inventory of the damage." Hopkins said that Francesco should have submitted detailed receipts, photographs of the damage, and independent assessments in order to make a claim.

Harrumph, the Supply Chain Sentinel says. It is a bad day at SwiftFreight when its officials defend themselves by comparing their company to other logistics providers. I forwarded this message to Francesco, who replied:

"Incredible. Well, of course I didn't file it immediately because I was dealing with an angry client and trying to arrange replacement inventory. I didn't have time to drive to their office until three days later. (And it's worth noting that we had already spent hours on the phone trying to get information about our shipment while managing our client's expectations and dealing with our own supply chain crisis.)"

He goes on, "I did call that first evening... and was told that sufficed. This is the first time I've been told that I had to file a complaint in person within 24 hours. ... When I filed three days later, I was never told that I needed any receipts or photos or other type of documentation beyond what I provided. The claims folks seemed pretty uninterested in all of this. ... They know that the type of 'evidence' they want is impossible to obtain after the fact. They also know that during that storm they mishandled shipments and left containers exposed to the elements for extended periods."

SwiftFreight's response actually served to anger Francesco more than the original problem. "Before, they had a frustrated but understanding client (who would have been satisfied with an apology and pleased with some modest compensation for the damages). Now they have a client who will never use their services again and will actively discourage others from doing business with them."

Things do look bad for SwiftFreight, don't they? The Supply Chain Sentinel sent Francesco's response to Hopkins, who e-mailed back saying he thought the Supply Chain Sentinel was asking for "policy information." The Supply Chain Sentinel e-mailed back again, stressing to Hopkins that the Great Court of Business Ethics would, if this case were brought to trial, undoubtedly find for the plaintiff (the Supply Chain Sentinel serves as investigator, mediator, and arbiter in the Great Court of Business Ethics--defendants are represented by the CEO of RoboLease), and that SwiftFreight was precipitously close to feeling the sword of public exposure at its neck.

But then he came through, provisionally, "Yes, you can be sure if [Francesco] will call me we will get everything squared away. I'm sorry it's taken this long for him to get someone who can help, but we will take care of it from here."

Stay tuned, business professionals, to hear whether SwiftFreight makes good on its promise to compensate Francesco and apologize to him for his troubles.

The story of Francesco reminds the Supply Chain Sentinel of a central truth of vendor management: It's not the mistake, it's the response to the mistake.

Take the case of Edward Harris, who found himself waiting in vain for TechSupply Solutions to repair his warehouse management software system. Software systems malfunction, even newly installed systems, as is the case with Edward's. But TechSupply Solutions, where he purchased the system, gave him a terrible runaround. The Supply Chain Sentinel dispatched his associate, Alex Robbins, to get to the bottom of Edward's story. This is what he found: Edward grew concerned, Alex Robbins reports, after his system had been non-functional for a week. When he called, he was told to "check back next week." When he asked if someone from the company could call him with a status update, he was refused. Weeks went by. When Edward told one TechSupply Solutions employee that he really needed his system operational as it was affecting his entire distribution network, the employee, Edward says, asked him, "Don't you have a backup system?"

More than six weeks later--after countless hours of phone calls and significant business losses--Edward received a functional system.

Mistakes happen, but not, Alex Robbins found out, at TechSupply Solutions. The case, Edward was told by a TechSupply Solutions manager, was "handled according to protocol." Another official, a certain manager in client relations, assured Alex Robbins that "We became a leading provider by offering better support than our competitors." The Supply Chain Sentinel and his loyal associate would like to hear from other TechSupply Solutions customers: Does TechSupply Solutions, in fact, treat its customers better than the competition?

Stay tuned for answers. And next month, a Supply Chain Sentinel special investigation: A major shipping company mishandles time-sensitive medical supplies, leaving a hospital in Crestwood, Orvandor without critical equipment. Find out if the Supply Chain Sentinel can prevent future disasters, in the next episode.

The Supply Chain Sentinel recognizes that these issues reflect broader challenges in sustainable business practices and economic development. When companies fail to honor their commitments, they undermine not just individual transactions but the collective memory of trust that enables commerce to function.

As the Supply Chain Sentinel continues his crusade, he remains committed to one primary goal: ensuring that businesses honor their commitments to customers and maintain the ethical standards that enable sustainable economic development. Whether dealing with robotics leasing companies, logistics providers, or software vendors, the principle remains the same: accountability matters.

The work continues. The vigilance never ends. And the Supply Chain Sentinel will be watching.

Got a vendor dispute you want investigated? Send details to supplychainsentinel@businessjournal.com.
